claims.quote: Early frameworks demonstrated that sequence-based generative models could be steered toward desirable chemical properties through reinforcement learning; Olivecrona and colleagues showed that augmented episodic likelihood enables a recurrent model to produce analogues of query structures and to generate compounds predicted to be active against specific biological targets [arxiv_1704.07555].

Gao and Coley systematically evaluated this limitation, demonstrating that a substantial fraction of molecules proposed by leading generative frameworks cannot be readily accessed through known synthetic routes, thereby undermining their translational value [arxiv_2002.07007].

The GuacaMol benchmarking framework was introduced specifically to address the related problem of inconsistent evaluation protocols, providing standardized tasks against which neural generative models can be systematically profiled and compared to established computational chemistry baselines [arxiv_1811.09621].

Flow-based autoregressive models operating directly on molecular graphs address the dual challenge of producing chemically valid structures while simultaneously optimizing chemical properties [arxiv_2001.09382]. More recently, transformer architectures have been adapted for de novo design, with joint transformer frameworks combining decoder, encoder, and predictor components in a shared-weight generative model that formulates molecular generation as a probabilistic black-box optimization problem, explicitly targeting the difficulty of generating novel molecules outside the training distribution [arxiv_2310.02066].

Traditional QSAR methods rely on handcrafted molecular descriptors, as exemplified by [arxiv_1904.05052], which employs protein star graph descriptors combined with classical ML classifiers to categorize signaling proteins relevant to drug targets.

In contrast, deep neural networks that perform feature learning directly from molecular structure promise to outperform both traditional physics-based and knowledge-based approaches by circumventing the limitations of manual feature engineering [arxiv_1803.04465]. PotentialNet, introduced in that work, is specifically designed to capture molecular properties across multiple length scales, from solubility to protein–ligand binding, using staged graph convolutional networks that encode both covalent and non-covalent interactions.

Directed message-passing neural networks have been shown to construct expressive learned molecular representations that compare favorably to models relying on pre-computed fingerprints or expert-crafted descriptors [arxiv_1904.01561]. Subsequent architectural refinements sought to balance expressiveness with computational efficiency; multiplex graph formulations incorporated molecular mechanics information to improve predictive accuracy [arxiv_2011.07457], while attention-based directed message passing further refined how structural information is aggregated across molecular graphs [arxiv_2305.14819].

A meta-learning perspective on QSAR, wherein knowledge accumulated across many target-specific datasets is leveraged to improve predictions on new, data-scarce targets, has been advanced by Meta-QSAR [arxiv_1709.03854] and meta-learning GNN initializations [arxiv_2003.05996], the latter specifically targeting low-resource molecular property prediction.

Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) applied directly to three-dimensional representations of protein–ligand complexes can learn scoring functions capable of ranking binding affinities and poses, leveraging the growing availability of structural and binding data to outperform several classical scoring approaches [arxiv_1612.02751].

A dual-graph convolutional network that separately encodes ligand bonded topology and ligand–protein contacts derived from docking poses demonstrates that combining structural rank information with deep learning improves binding mode prediction [arxiv_1910.02845].

MolCLR [arxiv_2102.10056] exemplifies this direction by applying contrastive learning over molecular graphs via graph neural networks, leveraging augmentation strategies to learn transferable representations without requiring extensive labeled datasets.

Graph Self-Supervised Learning (GSSL) addresses the labeled-data bottleneck by acquiring molecular embeddings without expert labeling, with its primary strength lying in transferability across domains [arxiv_2206.08005].
